title: The “Do Now” Dilemma: Fixing the Ragged Start
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Opening a series on the “microscopic lesson moves” that decide whether a lesson flies or flops, Emanuele examines the Do Now—the settling starter task on the board as students arrive. The theory is well established (accessible, disconnected retrieval practice, brief), but the reality is a “ragged start” created by students trickling in at different times: punctual pupils finish and drift, latecomers never catch up, and the quiet the teacher fought to build leaks away. Emanuele describes how greeting students at the door and offering extension tasks failed to solve this, and sets up a specific entry routine that synchronises the class so the majority start, settle, and finish the Do Now together regardless of arrival time.
points: The Do Now is treated as the most critical moment of the lesson—one of the small mechanics that determine whether a lesson succeeds.
Good starters follow three rules: accessibility (no equipment needed), disconnection (retrieval or interleaving, not the current topic), and brevity (five questions maximum).
The core problem is the “ragged start”: staggered arrivals mean punctual students finish and wait while latecomers never settle, destroying momentum.
Common fixes fail—extension tasks leave the room unsettled, and greeting students individually at the door lets the room’s energy leak out.
The proposed solution is a specific entry routine that synchronises when the class starts, settles, and finishes the Do Now, regardless of when each student arrives.
quotes: I want to “deep dive” into the specific mechanics of teaching, the microscopic lesson moves that determine whether a lesson flies or flops
It should be retrieval or interleave practice, disconnected from the current topic to build memory retention.
If you move on to marking the do now, you lose the latecomers. If you wait for the latecomers, you lose the momentum of the punctual students
I realised that by staying at the door greeting students individually as they trickled in, I was inadvertently allowing the energy of the room to leak out.

It ensures at least the vast majority of the class (if not the whole) starts at the same time, settles at the same time, and finishes the Do Now at the same time, regardless of when they arrived at my door.
